tool.name: PostgreSQL
tool.tagline: Advanced open-source relational database with rich types and extensions
tool.description: PostgreSQL is a powerful open-source relational database known for correctness, standards compliance and extensibility. Beyond standard SQL it offers jsonb, arrays, ranges, full-text search, many index types and an extension ecosystem (PostGIS, pgvector), and it is the default database for many web back ends. This curriculum covers using it day to day through to operating, tuning and replicating it.

concepts.name: Installing PostgreSQL and psql
concepts.summary: Install a PostgreSQL server, connect with the psql client and run your first queries.
concepts.why: psql is the tool every PostgreSQL user, DBA and tutorial relies on, and a local server is where you learn safely.
concepts.body:
PostgreSQL is a **client-server** database: a server process (`postgres`) manages the data directory and accepts connections, and clients such as `psql`, GUI tools or your application connect to it over TCP (port 5432 by default) or a Unix socket.

Ways to get a server running:

- **Docker** is the quickest: `docker run --name pg -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret -p 5432:5432 -d postgres:18`.
- **Packages**: the PostgreSQL project's apt/yum repositories, Postgres.app or Homebrew on macOS, the EDB installer on Windows.
- **Managed services** (Amazon RDS/Aurora, Google Cloud SQL, Azure, Neon, Supabase) for production.

A fresh installation has a superuser role called `postgres` and a database also called `postgres`. Connect with `psql`, the interactive terminal: `psql -h localhost -U postgres`. At the `postgres=#` prompt you can type SQL terminated by `;`, or **meta-commands** that start with a backslash and are handled by psql itself: `\l` lists databases, `\c dbname` connects to another, `\dt` lists tables, `\d name` describes a table, `\?` shows help and `\q` quits.

Create a database for each project instead of working in `postgres`, and create a non-superuser role for your application — the superuser bypasses every permission check.
concepts.code:
# start a throwaway server (data is lost when the container is removed)
docker run --name pg -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret -p 5432:5432 -d postgres:18

psql -h localhost -U postgres          # prompts for the password
# postgres=# SELECT version();
# postgres=# CREATE DATABASE shop;
# postgres=# \c shop
# You are now connected to database "shop" as user "postgres".
# shop=# CREATE TABLE product (id int PRIMARY KEY, name text);
# shop=# \dt
#          List of relations
#  Schema |  Name   | Type  |  Owner
#  public | product | table | postgres
# shop=# \q
takeaways: The server owns the data; psql and apps are clients
Backslash commands (\l, \c, \dt, \d) are psql features, not SQL
Use a database per project and a non-superuser role for apps
pitfalls: Forgetting the semicolon: psql keeps waiting for more input and the prompt changes to postgres-#.

quiz.q: Which of these is handled by psql itself rather than sent to the server as SQL?
quiz.explain: Backslash meta-commands are interpreted by the psql client, which runs catalog queries for you.

concepts.name: psql productivity
concepts.summary: Use psql's describe commands, expanded output, timing, variables and script files to work fast.
concepts.why: Fluency in psql makes exploring schemas and debugging production databases much quicker than any GUI.
concepts.body:
psql is far more than a prompt. The commands worth memorising:

- **Describe**: `\d table` (columns, indexes, constraints), `\d+` (plus sizes and storage), `\dn` schemas, `\du` roles, `\df` functions, `\di` indexes, `\dx` extensions. Add a pattern: `\dt sales.*`.
- **Output**: `\x auto` switches to one-column-per-line display when rows are too wide; `\pset null '(null)'` makes NULLs visible.
- **Timing**: `\timing on` prints how long each statement took.
- **Editing**: `\e` opens the last query in `$EDITOR`; `\ef func` edits a function.
- **Scripts**: `\i file.sql` runs a file; from the shell, `psql -f file.sql` does the same, and `-v ON_ERROR_STOP=1` stops at the first error (always use it in automation).
- **Variables**: `\set id 42` then `SELECT * FROM t WHERE id = :id;` — or `:'name'` for a quoted literal.
- **Re-running**: `\watch 2` repeats the last query every two seconds, handy for monitoring.
- **Exporting**: `\copy` (next lessons) and `\o file` to redirect output.

Settings you want every time go in `~/.psqlrc`. `\set ECHO_HIDDEN on` shows the catalog queries behind `\d` commands — a great way to learn the system catalogs.
concepts.code:
# ~/.psqlrc
\set QUIET 1
\x auto
\timing on
\pset null '(null)'
\set ON_ERROR_STOP on
\set QUIET 0

# run a migration script safely from the shell
psql "postgresql://app@localhost/shop" -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -f migrate.sql

# inside psql
# shop=# \set uid 42
# shop=# SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = :uid;
# shop=# SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity \watch 5
takeaways: \d, \d+, \dn, \du, \df, \di describe objects
\x auto and \timing on belong in every ~/.psqlrc
Run scripts with -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 so failures stop the script
pitfalls: Running psql -f in CI without ON_ERROR_STOP, so a failed statement is ignored and the script 'succeeds'.

quiz.q: You run psql -f migrate.sql and statement 3 of 10 fails. Without ON_ERROR_STOP, what happens?
options: psql reports the error and continues with statements 4 to 10
psql stops and rolls back everything
quiz.explain: By default psql prints the error and carries on, which is why automation should set ON_ERROR_STOP.

concepts.name: Clusters, databases and schemas
concepts.summary: How a PostgreSQL cluster contains databases, databases contain schemas, and search_path resolves names.
concepts.why: Namespacing decides what queries see and is the basis of permissions and multi-tenant layouts.
concepts.body:
PostgreSQL organises objects in three levels:

- A **cluster** (instance) is one running server with one data directory. It holds several databases and the **roles** shared by all of them.
- A **database** is isolated: a connection belongs to exactly one database and can't query tables in another (you'd need `postgres_fdw` or dblink). Use separate databases for separate applications.
- A **schema** is a namespace *inside* a database, holding tables, views, functions and types. Objects in different schemas of the same database can be joined freely. Every database starts with a `public` schema.

Unqualified names are resolved through the **search_path** setting, by default `"$user", public`: first a schema named after your role (if it exists), then `public`. So `SELECT * FROM orders` finds `public.orders` unless you have a `yourname.orders`. You can always qualify: `sales.orders`.

Schemas are useful to group an application's areas (`billing`, `audit`), to install extensions out of the way, or to give each tenant its own namespace. Since PostgreSQL 15, ordinary users can no longer create objects in `public` by default — the owner of the database must grant `CREATE` or you create your own schema. Set `search_path` per role or per database (`ALTER ROLE app SET search_path = app, public`) rather than in every session.
takeaways: Cluster > database > schema > table
Connections are per database; schemas in one database can be joined
search_path decides which schema an unqualified name means
pitfalls: Expecting to join tables across two databases in one query.

quiz.q: search_path is billing, public and both schemas have a table called invoice. What does SELECT * FROM invoice read?
quiz.explain: Names resolve to the first schema in search_path that contains a matching object.

concepts.name: Connecting applications
concepts.summary: Connection URIs, libpq environment variables, pg_hba.conf authentication and drivers for your language.
concepts.why: Most 'can't connect' problems come down to the URI, pg_hba.conf or SSL settings covered here.
concepts.body:
Applications connect with a driver: `psycopg` (Python), `pg` / `postgres` (Node.js), `pgx` (Go), the JDBC driver (Java), `Npgsql` (.NET). Almost all accept a **connection URI**:

`postgresql://user:password@host:5432/dbname?sslmode=require`

Tools built on libpq (psql, pg_dump) also read **environment variables** such as `PGHOST`, `PGPORT`, `PGUSER`, `PGDATABASE` and `PGPASSWORD`, and a `~/.pgpass` file for passwords, so secrets don't end up in shell history.

On the server two layers decide whether a connection is accepted:

- `listen_addresses` in `postgresql.conf` controls which network interfaces the server listens on (default `localhost` in most packages; the Docker image listens on all).
- `pg_hba.conf` ("host-based authentication") is an ordered list of rules: connection type, database, user, client address, and method — `scram-sha-256` for passwords, `peer` for local OS users, `cert` for client certificates. The first matching line wins; reload the server after editing.

Practical rules: use one role per application with only the privileges it needs; require TLS (`sslmode=require` or `verify-full`) for anything crossing a network; and keep the number of connections modest — each one is a server process, so use a pool in the application (and possibly PgBouncer) instead of opening a connection per request.
concepts.code:
# Python with psycopg 3:  pip install "psycopg[binary]"
import psycopg

url = "postgresql://app:secret@localhost:5432/shop"
with psycopg.connect(url) as conn:              # commits on clean exit
    with conn.cursor() as cur:
        cur.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS note (id serial PRIMARY KEY, body text)")
        cur.execute("INSERT INTO note (body) VALUES (%s) RETURNING id", ("hello",))
        print(cur.fetchone())                  # (1,)
        cur.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM note WHERE body = %s", ("hello",))
        print(cur.fetchone()[0])               # 1

# pg_hba.conf line: allow app from the app subnet with password auth
# host  shop  app  10.0.0.0/24  scram-sha-256
takeaways: Connection URI: postgresql://user:pass@host:port/db?sslmode=...
pg_hba.conf rules are matched top to bottom; reload after changes
Always pass values as parameters, never by string formatting
pitfalls: Building SQL with f-strings, which opens the door to SQL injection.

quiz.q: A client gets 'no pg_hba.conf entry for host'. What needs to change?
options: A rule in pg_hba.conf allowing that host, user and database
quiz.explain: The server reached authentication but found no matching pg_hba.conf rule for that connection.

concepts.name: Choosing core data types
concepts.summary: Pick PostgreSQL types well: text vs varchar, integer sizes, numeric vs float, boolean and bytea.
concepts.why: Types are hard to change on big tables, and the right ones prevent bugs like rounding errors in money.
concepts.body:
PostgreSQL has a rich type system; a few choices cover most columns.

- **Text**: use `text`. `varchar(n)` is the same type with a length check, and `char(n)` pads with spaces — avoid it. If you need a limit, a `CHECK (length(x) <= n)` is easier to change later. Performance is identical.
- **Integers**: `integer` (4 bytes, up to about 2.1 billion) and `bigint` (8 bytes). Use `bigint` for primary keys of tables that may grow large; running out of `integer` ids is a classic outage. `smallint` rarely pays off.
- **Exact decimals**: `numeric(p, s)` for money and anything that must add up exactly. `real` and `double precision` are binary floating point: fast, approximate, fine for measurements. Avoid the `money` type; it depends on the `lc_monetary` setting.
- **boolean**: `true`, `false` or `NULL`.
- **Binary**: `bytea`. For large files, store them in object storage and keep the path.
- **Dates and times**: `date`, and `timestamptz` (next lessons).

Also useful: `uuid`, `jsonb`, arrays, `inet`/`cidr` for IP addresses, and range types — covered later. Use the `::` operator (or standard `CAST`) to convert: `'42'::int`. `pg_typeof(expr)` tells you the type of any expression, which is handy when an operator complains it doesn't exist for your types.
takeaways: text everywhere; add a CHECK if you need a max length
bigint for ids that may grow; numeric for money
Floats are approximate; never compare them for exact equality
pitfalls: Using integer primary keys on a fast-growing table and hitting 2,147,483,647.

quiz.q: Which type should store invoice totals?
quiz.explain: numeric is exact decimal arithmetic; floats round, and money depends on locale settings.

concepts.name: Identity columns and UUIDs
concepts.summary: Generate keys with GENERATED AS IDENTITY instead of serial, or with gen_random_uuid() and uuidv7().
concepts.why: Every table needs a key generator, and the modern options avoid serial's permission and ownership quirks.
concepts.body:
The modern way to auto-generate integer keys is an **identity column**, standard SQL since PostgreSQL 10:

- `GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` rejects explicit values unless you write `OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE` — good protection against accidental manual ids.
- `GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY` uses the sequence unless you supply a value — convenient for imports.

You'll still see the older `serial` / `bigserial` pseudo-types. They create a separate sequence plus a default, which causes quirks with permissions and copying table definitions; prefer identity in new schemas.

Both are backed by a **sequence**, which hands out numbers without waiting for transactions to finish. Consequence: a rolled-back insert still consumes its number, so ids have **gaps**. Never rely on ids being contiguous or use them as a count.

For **UUIDs**, use the `uuid` type (16 bytes, not text). `gen_random_uuid()` (built in since 13) gives random version-4 UUIDs. PostgreSQL 18 adds `uuidv7()`, which is time-ordered: new values sort after older ones, so B-tree inserts stay at the right edge of the index instead of landing at random pages. Prefer v7 for primary keys when you choose UUIDs.

After a bulk load with explicit ids, move the sequence past the maximum with `setval`, or the next insert will collide.
takeaways: Prefer GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY over serial
Sequences never roll back, so ids have gaps
Store UUIDs in the uuid type; uuidv7() keeps inserts index-friendly
pitfalls: Storing UUIDs as text, which doubles their size and slows comparisons.

quiz.q: A transaction inserts a row into an identity table and then rolls back. What happens to the generated id?
options: It is reused by the next insert
It is consumed, leaving a gap
quiz.explain: Sequence increments are not transactional, so the number is gone even though the row isn't.

concepts.name: Timestamps and time zones
concepts.summary: Store moments in time as timestamptz, understand the TimeZone setting, and do interval arithmetic.
concepts.why: Time zone bugs are among the most common data bugs; one rule about timestamptz prevents most of them.
concepts.body:
PostgreSQL has two timestamp types, and the names mislead:

- `timestamp with time zone` (**timestamptz**) stores an absolute instant, internally in UTC. On input, a value without an offset is interpreted in the session's `TimeZone`; on output it is converted to the session's `TimeZone`. It does *not* store the original zone.
- `timestamp` (without time zone) stores a wall-clock reading with no zone at all. `2026-03-29 02:30` means nothing until you say where.

Rule: use **timestamptz** for events that happened at a moment (created_at, paid_at). Use `timestamp` or `date` + `time` only for civil times that must not shift, such as "the shop opens at 09:00 local time", and store the zone name in another column.

Useful tools:

- `now()` returns the transaction's start time; `clock_timestamp()` the actual current time.
- `AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Yerevan'` converts a timestamptz into local wall-clock time in that zone (and the reverse for a plain timestamp).
- `interval` arithmetic: `now() - interval '7 days'`, `age(a, b)`.
- `date_trunc('day', ts)` for bucketing — it truncates in the session time zone.

Set the server or database `TimeZone` to UTC and convert at the edges, in the application or with `AT TIME ZONE`.
takeaways: timestamptz stores an instant (UTC) and displays it in the session TimeZone
Use timestamptz for events; plain timestamp only for zone-less civil times
AT TIME ZONE converts between instants and local wall-clock times
pitfalls: Using timestamp without time zone for created_at and getting shifted values when servers or sessions change zone.

quiz.q: A timestamptz column holds 12:00 UTC. A session with TimeZone = 'Europe/Paris' (UTC+1 in winter) selects it in January. What is shown?
quiz.explain: The same instant is displayed converted to the session's time zone.

concepts.name: RETURNING and upserts
concepts.summary: Get generated values back from INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE with RETURNING, and combine it with ON CONFLICT.
concepts.why: RETURNING saves a round trip and avoids race-prone 'insert then select' code.
concepts.body:
PostgreSQL's `RETURNING` clause makes data-modifying statements return rows, like a `SELECT` of what they just changed:

- `INSERT ... RETURNING id` gives you generated keys and defaults without a second query.
- `UPDATE ... RETURNING *` shows the new values after the update.
- `DELETE ... RETURNING *` returns what was removed — handy for moving rows to an archive table.

PostgreSQL 18 also lets you write `RETURNING old.col, new.col` to see both the before and after values of an update.

Combined with **upsert** (`INSERT ... ON CONFLICT`), it becomes very expressive. `ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE SET col = EXCLUDED.col` inserts a new row or updates the existing one atomically; `EXCLUDED` refers to the row you tried to insert. `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` skips duplicates — but note that then `RETURNING` returns no row for the skipped ones.

Data-modifying statements can also sit inside a `WITH` clause, and the outer query can use their `RETURNING` output. That lets you, for example, delete old rows and insert them into an archive in a single statement.

`ON CONFLICT` needs a unique index or constraint on the conflict target columns; it is the safe, concurrent alternative to "SELECT, and INSERT if missing".
concepts.code:
CREATE TABLE stock (sku text PRIMARY KEY, qty int NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE stock_archive (sku text, qty int, archived_at timestamptz DEFAULT now());

INSERT INTO stock VALUES ('A1', 5) RETURNING *;            -- A1 | 5

INSERT INTO stock VALUES ('A1', 3)
ON CONFLICT (sku) DO UPDATE SET qty = stock.qty + EXCLUDED.qty
RETURNING sku, qty;                                         -- A1 | 8

UPDATE stock SET qty = 0 WHERE sku = 'A1' RETURNING qty;    -- 0

WITH gone AS (
    DELETE FROM stock WHERE qty = 0 RETURNING sku, qty
)
INSERT INTO stock_archive (sku, qty) SELECT sku, qty FROM gone
RETURNING sku;                                              -- A1
takeaways: RETURNING turns INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE into row-producing statements
ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE with EXCLUDED is an atomic upsert
Data-modifying CTEs chain changes in one statement
pitfalls: Expecting RETURNING to produce a row for inputs skipped by ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING.

quiz.q: In ON CONFLICT (sku) DO UPDATE SET qty = EXCLUDED.qty, what is EXCLUDED?
options: The row already in the table
The row that was proposed for insertion
quiz.explain: EXCLUDED holds the values you tried to insert; the table name refers to the existing row.

concepts.name: Bulk loading with COPY
concepts.summary: Load and export CSV fast with COPY on the server or \copy from psql.
concepts.why: COPY is an order of magnitude faster than row-by-row INSERTs for imports, exports and data fixes.
concepts.body:
`COPY` moves data between a table (or query) and a file or stream in one efficient operation. It is the fastest way to load data into PostgreSQL — typically many times faster than individual `INSERT` statements, because it avoids per-statement parsing and network round trips.

There are two flavours that look alike:

- `COPY table FROM '/path/file.csv'` runs **on the server**: the path is on the database server's filesystem, and you need superuser or the `pg_read_server_files` / `pg_write_server_files` roles. Useless for a managed database where you can't reach the server's disk.
- `\copy table FROM 'file.csv'` is a **psql** command: psql reads the file on *your* machine and streams it through `COPY ... FROM STDIN`. Same options, ordinary privileges. This is what you usually want.

Common options: `(FORMAT csv, HEADER true)`, `DELIMITER`, `NULL ''`, and a column list to load only some columns. To export a query result: `\copy (SELECT ...) TO 'out.csv' (FORMAT csv, HEADER)`.

`COPY` is all-or-nothing: one malformed row aborts the whole load (PostgreSQL 17 added `ON_ERROR ignore` to skip rows with conversion errors). A robust pattern for messy files is to load into a staging table of `text` columns, clean with SQL, then `INSERT ... SELECT` into the real table. Drivers expose COPY too, for example `cursor.copy()` in psycopg 3.
concepts.code:
# products.csv
# sku,name,price
# A1,Pen,1.50
# B2,Notebook,4.00

psql shop <<'SQL'
CREATE TABLE product (sku text PRIMARY KEY, name text, price numeric(8,2));
\copy product FROM 'products.csv' WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER true)
SELECT count(*) FROM product;
-- 2
\copy (SELECT sku, price * 1.2 AS price_vat FROM product) TO 'vat.csv' WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER)
SQL
takeaways: COPY is the fast path for bulk import and export
COPY reads files on the server; \copy reads them on the client
Load messy data into a text staging table, then clean with SQL
pitfalls: Using server-side COPY with a path on your laptop and getting 'could not open file'.

quiz.q: You're connected with psql to a managed cloud database and want to load data.csv from your laptop. What do you use?
quiz.explain: \copy streams the local file through the connection; server-side COPY looks on the server's disk.

concepts.name: Roles and privileges
concepts.summary: Create login and group roles, GRANT the minimum privileges, and set default privileges for future tables.
concepts.why: Least-privilege roles limit the damage of a leaked password or an SQL injection bug.
concepts.body:
In PostgreSQL users and groups are both **roles**. A role with `LOGIN` can connect; a role without it acts as a group that others are granted membership in. Roles are cluster-wide, shared by all databases.

Privileges are granted on objects:

- `GRANT CONNECT ON DATABASE shop TO app;`
- `GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA app TO app;` — needed to see anything inside the schema.
- `GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA app TO app;`
- `GRANT USAGE ON ALL SEQUENCES IN SCHEMA app TO app;` for `serial` columns.

`ON ALL TABLES` only covers tables that exist now. For future tables, use `ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES` — it applies to objects created later *by the role that runs it* (or `FOR ROLE owner`).

A clean pattern: a **owner** role (`app_owner`, no login) owns the schema and runs migrations; group roles `app_rw` and `app_ro` hold read-write and read-only privileges; login roles for services and people are members of those groups. Avoid letting the application connect as the owner or as a superuser: owners can drop tables and superusers bypass all checks, including row-level security.

Since PostgreSQL 14 the predefined roles `pg_read_all_data` and `pg_write_all_data` make read-only analytics users easy. Use `\du` and `\dp` in psql to inspect roles and table privileges.
takeaways: Users and groups are both roles; LOGIN makes a role a user
Schema USAGE plus table privileges are both needed
ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES covers tables created in the future
pitfalls: Granting on ALL TABLES once and wondering why new tables are inaccessible.

quiz.q: A role has SELECT on app.orders but queries fail with 'permission denied for schema app'. What's missing?
quiz.explain: Objects inside a schema can't be reached without USAGE on the schema itself.

concepts.name: jsonb in practice
concepts.summary: Query, update and index jsonb documents with ->, ->>, @>, jsonb_set and SQL/JSON functions.
concepts.why: jsonb lets one relational database also handle flexible, document-style data without a second system.
concepts.body:
PostgreSQL has two JSON types. `json` stores the text verbatim; **jsonb** stores a parsed binary form — keys de-duplicated, whitespace dropped — that is faster to query and can be indexed. Use `jsonb`.

Reading:

- `doc -> 'key'` returns jsonb; `doc ->> 'key'` returns text. Chain them: `doc -> 'address' ->> 'city'`, or use a path: `doc #>> '{address,city}'`.
- `doc @> '{"plan": "pro"}'` tests containment and can use a GIN index.
- `doc ? 'key'` tests if a top-level key exists.
- `jsonb_array_elements(doc -> 'items')` turns an array into rows; `jsonb_to_recordset` turns an array of objects into typed rows.
- SQL/JSON path: `jsonb_path_query(doc, '$.items[*] ? (@.qty > 1)')`; PostgreSQL 17 adds the standard `JSON_TABLE`.

Writing: `jsonb_set(doc, '{address,city}', '"Gyumri"')` replaces a nested value, `doc || '{"vip": true}'` merges top-level keys, and `doc - 'key'` removes one. Each update rewrites the whole value, so large documents that change often are costly.

Use jsonb for genuinely variable attributes, payloads from external APIs and settings. Anything you filter, join or constrain regularly deserves a real column — with types, constraints and normal statistics for the planner.
takeaways: -> returns jsonb, ->> returns text
@> containment queries can use a GIN index
Promote frequently filtered fields to real columns
pitfalls: Comparing profile -> 'age' > 30: -> returns jsonb, so cast (profile ->> 'age')::int instead.

quiz.q: What does profile ->> 'plan' return for {"plan": "pro"}?
quiz.explain: ->> extracts the field as text; -> would return the jsonb string "pro".

concepts.name: Arrays, enums and domains
concepts.summary: Use array columns with ANY and unnest, enum types for fixed value sets, and domains for reusable constraints.
concepts.why: These PostgreSQL types model common patterns concisely, as long as you know where each one stops fitting.
concepts.body:
**Arrays**: any type can be an array, e.g. `text[]`. Literals look like `'{a,b}'` or `ARRAY['a','b']`. Useful operators: `'x' = ANY(tags)`, containment `tags @> ARRAY['x']` (GIN-indexable), overlap `&&`, `array_length(tags, 1)`, and `unnest(tags)` to turn an array into rows; `array_agg` goes the other way. Arrays are 1-based. Good for small lists of tags or values you read together; if you need foreign keys or per-item attributes, use a child table.

**Enums**: `CREATE TYPE mood AS ENUM ('sad', 'ok', 'happy')`. Values are stored compactly and sort in declaration order. You can add values (`ALTER TYPE mood ADD VALUE 'ecstatic' AFTER 'happy'`), but removing or renaming is awkward. For sets that change often, a lookup table or a `CHECK` constraint is more flexible.

**Domains**: a named type with constraints, reusable across tables: `CREATE DOMAIN email AS text CHECK (VALUE ~ '^[^@]+@[^@]+$')`. Changing the rule in one place updates every column using it.

All three are PostgreSQL extensions to standard SQL (arrays are partly standard), so they tie you a little more to PostgreSQL — usually a fine trade.
takeaways: Arrays: = ANY(), @>, && and unnest; 1-based
Enums sort in declaration order and are hard to shrink
Domains are reusable constrained types
pitfalls: Using an array of ids instead of a junction table, losing foreign keys.

quiz.q: Which query finds tickets whose tags include 'bug'?
quiz.explain: = ANY(array) tests whether any element equals the value.

concepts.name: Partial, expression and concurrent indexes
concepts.summary: Build indexes without blocking writes, index expressions and subsets of rows, and find unused indexes.
concepts.why: These options make indexes smaller, more targeted and safe to create on a live production table.
concepts.body:
A plain `CREATE INDEX` blocks writes to the table until it finishes — minutes or hours on a big table. In production use **`CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`**: it builds without blocking inserts, updates and deletes, at the cost of taking longer and scanning the table twice. It can't run inside a transaction block, and if it fails it leaves an `INVALID` index you must drop and retry. `REINDEX CONCURRENTLY` and `DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY` exist too.

**Expression indexes** index the result of an expression, so queries using that same expression can use them: `CREATE INDEX ON users (lower(email))` serves `WHERE lower(email) = $1`. The query must match the expression exactly.

**Partial indexes** include only rows matching a `WHERE` clause: `CREATE INDEX ON orders (created_at) WHERE status = 'pending'` stays tiny when most orders are completed. A partial *unique* index enforces uniqueness on a subset, for example one active subscription per user.

Combine with `INCLUDE (cols)` for covering index-only scans. To find dead weight, check `pg_stat_user_indexes`: an index with `idx_scan = 0` over weeks (on the primary and every replica) is a candidate to drop. Every index slows writes and takes cache space, so keep the set lean.
takeaways: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY avoids blocking writes; check for INVALID leftovers
Expression indexes need the query to use the same expression
Partial indexes are small and can enforce conditional uniqueness
pitfalls: Running CREATE INDEX (without CONCURRENTLY) on a large hot table during business hours.

quiz.q: An index exists on lower(email). Which WHERE clause can use it?
quiz.explain: Only a predicate on the identical expression lower(email) matches the expression index.

concepts.name: EXPLAIN ANALYZE with BUFFERS
concepts.summary: Read PostgreSQL plans with timing and buffer counts, spot misestimates and catch slow plans with auto_explain.
concepts.why: Buffers show how much data a query touches, which is usually the real cost behind slow queries.
concepts.body:
`EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` runs the query and shows, per plan node, the estimated vs actual rows, timing, and **buffers**: how many 8 kB pages were read from PostgreSQL's cache (`shared hit`) or from the OS/disk (`read`). From PostgreSQL 18, `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` includes buffers by default.

How to read a plan:

- Read it inside-out: the most indented nodes run first and feed their parents.
- `actual time=a..b` is in milliseconds per loop; multiply by `loops` for nested nodes.
- Compare `rows=` estimated vs actual. Off by 10x or more means statistics or a predicate the planner can't estimate.
- `Rows Removed by Filter` large compared to rows returned suggests a missing or unusable index.
- Sorts or hashes that spill show `external merge Disk:` or `Batches: >1` — a sign `work_mem` is too small for that query.
- High `read` buffers means a cold cache or simply touching too much data.

Use `FORMAT JSON` and a visualiser (explain.dalibo.com, pgMustard) for big plans. To catch slow queries in production you can't reproduce, enable the **auto_explain** module with `auto_explain.log_min_duration`, which logs plans of slow statements automatically.

Remember `ANALYZE` executes the statement: wrap `UPDATE`/`DELETE` in `BEGIN; ... ROLLBACK;`.
takeaways: BUFFERS shows pages from cache (hit) and from disk (read)
Big estimate-vs-actual gaps and large Rows Removed by Filter point to the fix
auto_explain logs plans of slow queries in production
pitfalls: Timing a query twice and trusting the second, cached run as representative.

quiz.q: A Sort node shows 'Sort Method: external merge Disk: 120MB'. What does it suggest?
options: The sort exceeded work_mem and spilled to disk
quiz.explain: External merge means the data to sort didn't fit in work_mem for that operation.

concepts.name: Transactions in PostgreSQL
concepts.summary: Transactional DDL, savepoints, aborted transactions, and timeouts that protect the server from stuck sessions.
concepts.why: PostgreSQL's transaction behaviour differs from other databases in ways that affect migrations and error handling.
concepts.body:
A few PostgreSQL behaviours to know beyond `BEGIN`/`COMMIT`:

- **Transactional DDL**: `CREATE TABLE`, `ALTER TABLE` and most schema changes can be rolled back. A migration wrapped in a transaction either fully applies or leaves no trace — a big advantage over MySQL. Exceptions include `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, `VACUUM` and `CREATE DATABASE`.
- **Errors abort the transaction**: after any error inside a transaction, every further statement fails with "current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block" until you `ROLLBACK`.
- **Savepoints** let you recover part-way: `SAVEPOINT s1; ... ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT s1;` undoes only the work after the savepoint and clears the error. Drivers use them for nested transactions. They have a cost, so don't create thousands in a loop.
- The default isolation level is **Read Committed**; set others with `BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ` or `SERIALIZABLE`, and be ready to retry on SQLSTATE `40001`.

Protect the server with timeouts, set per role or database:

- `statement_timeout` cancels statements that run too long.
- `lock_timeout` stops a statement from waiting forever for a lock.
- `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` kills sessions that opened a transaction and went quiet; they hold locks and block VACUUM.
- `transaction_timeout` (PostgreSQL 17) caps a whole transaction.
takeaways: Most DDL is transactional in PostgreSQL
After an error, ROLLBACK (or roll back to a savepoint) before continuing
Set statement, lock and idle-in-transaction timeouts
pitfalls: Catching an exception in app code and continuing to use the same, now-aborted transaction.

quiz.q: Inside BEGIN ... you run CREATE TABLE x and then ROLLBACK. What happens to x in PostgreSQL?
options: x does not exist; the DDL was rolled back
x exists but is empty and locked
quiz.explain: PostgreSQL DDL is transactional, so the CREATE TABLE is undone with the rest.

concepts.name: SQL and PL/pgSQL functions
concepts.summary: Write SQL functions and PL/pgSQL functions and procedures with variables, control flow and exceptions.
concepts.why: Server-side functions keep data-heavy logic next to the data and are needed for triggers.
concepts.body:
PostgreSQL functions can be written in several languages. The two built-in ones:

- **SQL functions** (`LANGUAGE sql`) are one or more SQL statements; the result of the last is returned. Simple ones can be inlined into the calling query by the planner, so they're as fast as writing the SQL directly. Since PostgreSQL 14 you can write the body in standard form with `BEGIN ATOMIC ... END`.
- **PL/pgSQL** (`LANGUAGE plpgsql`) adds variables (`DECLARE`), `IF`, loops, `RAISE` for errors and notices, and `EXCEPTION` blocks. Use it when you need procedural logic.

Key options:

- Volatility: `IMMUTABLE` (same inputs, same output, no data access — required for expression indexes), `STABLE` (doesn't modify data, consistent within a statement), `VOLATILE` (default).
- `RETURNS TABLE (...)` or `RETURNS SETOF` to return rows; call it in `FROM`.
- `SECURITY DEFINER` runs with the owner's privileges — powerful, so also set `search_path` on the function.

**Procedures** (`CREATE PROCEDURE`, invoked with `CALL`) differ from functions in that they can `COMMIT` inside, which is useful for batch jobs that process data in chunks.

Keep business logic mostly in the application unless it's data-intensive or must be enforced for every writer; server code is harder to version, test and debug.
takeaways: LANGUAGE sql for simple, inlinable functions; plpgsql for procedural logic
Mark volatility correctly; IMMUTABLE is needed for index expressions
Procedures can COMMIT inside; functions cannot
pitfalls: Declaring a function IMMUTABLE when it reads tables, leading to stale or wrong results.

quiz.q: What happens to the first UPDATE when RAISE EXCEPTION fires inside the function?
options: It is saved in a savepoint for later
It is rolled back with the rest of the statement
Only the second UPDATE is undone
quiz.explain: An unhandled exception aborts the whole statement, undoing all its changes.

concepts.name: Materialized views
concepts.summary: Store a query's result with CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW and refresh it, concurrently, on a schedule.
concepts.why: Materialized views make expensive reports instant without building a separate summary pipeline.
concepts.body:
A regular view is just a saved query, executed each time you select from it. A **materialized view** runs the query once and stores the result like a table, so reading it is fast — at the cost of being stale until you refresh it.

- `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW daily_sales AS SELECT ...` creates and fills it (add `WITH NO DATA` to fill later).
- `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW daily_sales` recomputes it from scratch. It takes a lock that blocks reads while it runs.
- `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY daily_sales` computes the new result and applies the differences, so readers keep seeing the old data during the refresh. It requires a **unique index** on the materialized view and is slower overall.

You can index materialized views like tables, which is often the point: a pre-aggregated, indexed summary.

PostgreSQL has no built-in automatic or incremental refresh. Schedule refreshes with cron, the `pg_cron` extension or your job runner, and choose a frequency the business can accept as staleness. If you need always-current aggregates, maintain a summary table with triggers or in the application instead, or look at extensions for incremental view maintenance.

Good fits: dashboards, leaderboards, search facets, and expensive joins that change rarely compared with how often they're read.
takeaways: A materialized view stores the result and is stale until refreshed
REFRESH ... CONCURRENTLY keeps it readable but needs a unique index
Schedule refreshes yourself (cron, pg_cron)
pitfalls: Expecting a materialized view to update itself when the base tables change.

quiz.q: Why might REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY fail on a new materialized view?
quiz.explain: Concurrent refresh diffs old and new rows by a unique key, so a unique index is required.

concepts.name: Backups with pg_dump and pg_restore
concepts.summary: Take logical backups in custom or directory format, restore selectively and in parallel, and test restores.
concepts.why: A backup you haven't restored is a hope, not a backup; pg_dump is the everyday tool for it.
concepts.body:
**pg_dump** makes a *logical* backup of one database: SQL definitions and data, consistent as of the moment it started (it uses a snapshot, so it doesn't block normal reads and writes).

Formats:

- **plain** (`-Fp`, default): a SQL script you restore with `psql`. Readable, but all-or-nothing.
- **custom** (`-Fc`): compressed archive restored with **pg_restore**, which can restore selected tables (`-t`), list contents (`-l`), and run in parallel (`-j`). The usual choice.
- **directory** (`-Fd`): one file per table; supports parallel *dump* too (`-j 4`).

pg_dump covers one database and not cluster-wide objects. Roles and tablespaces come from `pg_dumpall --globals-only`.

Useful restore options: `--no-owner` and `--no-privileges` when restoring into an environment with different roles; `--clean --if-exists` to drop objects before recreating; `-d` to target a database. A newer pg_restore can read dumps from older servers, which makes dump/restore a simple (if slow) way to upgrade major versions.

Limits: for big databases, dump and restore take hours and you can only restore to the moment of the dump. Production systems combine physical backups with WAL archiving for point-in-time recovery (an Expert lesson). Whatever you use, **automate a regular test restore** and check the result.
concepts.code:
# custom-format dump of one database, plus cluster-wide roles
pg_dump -Fc -d shop -f shop.dump
pg_dumpall --globals-only -f globals.sql

# inspect, then restore into a fresh database with 4 parallel jobs
pg_restore -l shop.dump | head
createdb shop_restore
pg_restore -d shop_restore -j 4 --no-owner shop.dump

# restore only one table's data from the archive
pg_restore -d shop_restore -t orders --data-only shop.dump

# quick sanity check of the restore
psql -d shop_restore -c "SELECT count(*) FROM orders;"
takeaways: pg_dump is a consistent logical backup of one database
Use -Fc (or -Fd) to restore selectively and in parallel with pg_restore
Dump roles separately with pg_dumpall --globals-only and test restores
pitfalls: Backing up with pg_dump but never dumping roles, so restored privileges reference roles that don't exist.

quiz.q: Which pg_dump format lets pg_restore restore a single table and run with -j?
quiz.explain: Custom (and directory) archives are read by pg_restore, which supports selection and parallelism.

concepts.name: GIN, GiST, BRIN and operator classes
concepts.summary: Pick the right index access method for jsonb, arrays, text search, geometry and huge append-only tables.
concepts.why: When B-tree can't serve a query, choosing the right access method is the difference between seconds and milliseconds.
concepts.body:
PostgreSQL has several **index access methods**, each with **operator classes** that define which operators it accelerates.

- **GIN** (generalized inverted index) maps each element — array item, jsonb key/value, text-search lexeme, trigram — to the rows containing it. Use it for `@>`, `?`, `&&` and full-text `@@`. For jsonb, the `jsonb_path_ops` class is smaller and faster for `@>` but doesn't support `?`. GIN is slower to update; the `fastupdate` pending list batches inserts.
- **GiST** (generalized search tree) indexes things that overlap or have distance: geometry (PostGIS), ranges, nearest-neighbour `ORDER BY point <-> $1`. It powers exclusion constraints.
- **SP-GiST** suits space-partitioned data like points and IP prefixes.
- **BRIN** (block range index) stores only min/max per range of pages. It's tiny — kilobytes for a huge table — and works when values correlate with physical order, like `created_at` in an append-only log.
- **Hash**: equality only.

The **pg_trgm** extension adds trigram operator classes for GIN/GiST, making `LIKE '%term%'`, `ILIKE` and similarity search indexable — the usual answer to "my contains-search is slow".

Check which operators an index supports before creating it, and confirm with `EXPLAIN` that queries use it. Extensions such as pgvector add further methods (HNSW, IVFFlat) for vector similarity.
takeaways: GIN for containment in jsonb, arrays, text search and trigrams
GiST for ranges, geometry, nearest neighbour and exclusion constraints
BRIN is tiny and great for naturally ordered, append-only data
pitfalls: Creating BRIN on a column whose values are randomly distributed across the table.

quiz.q: Which index makes WHERE name ILIKE '%ova%' fast?
quiz.explain: Trigram GIN indexes break text into 3-character pieces, so substring searches can be answered from the index.

concepts.name: Range types and exclusion constraints
concepts.summary: Model intervals with tstzrange and daterange, query overlaps, and forbid overlapping bookings with EXCLUDE.
concepts.why: Double bookings are a classic race condition that an exclusion constraint prevents in one line.
concepts.body:
A **range type** stores an interval of values as one column: `int4range`, `numrange`, `daterange`, `tstzrange`. Bounds can be inclusive `[` or exclusive `)`; the convention `[start, end)` makes adjacent ranges meet without overlapping. Since PostgreSQL 14, **multiranges** hold sets of non-contiguous ranges.

Operators make interval logic simple and correct:

- `&&` overlaps, `@>` contains a value or range, `<@` is contained by.
- `-|-` adjacent, `*` intersection, `+` union.
- `lower(r)`, `upper(r)`, `isempty(r)`.

The killer feature is the **exclusion constraint**: `EXCLUDE USING gist (room WITH =, during WITH &&)` means "no two rows may have equal `room` *and* overlapping `during`". Like a unique constraint, it is enforced atomically, so two concurrent bookings for the same slot can't both succeed — something application checks can't guarantee without locking. Equality on a plain column inside a GiST index needs the `btree_gist` extension.

Ranges are useful for bookings, price validity periods, shift schedules and versioned (temporal) data. PostgreSQL 18 adds temporal `PRIMARY KEY`/`UNIQUE` constraints with `WITHOUT OVERLAPS`, building on the same idea.
takeaways: Range types store intervals; use [start, end) bounds
&& tests overlap, @> tests containment
EXCLUDE USING gist prevents overlapping rows atomically
pitfalls: Storing start and end in two columns and checking overlaps in application code, which races.

quiz.q: Ranges '[10:00, 12:00)' and '[12:00, 13:00)' for the same room. Does the exclusion constraint reject the second?
options: No, the first excludes 12:00 so they don't overlap
Only if the ranges are dates
quiz.explain: With an exclusive upper bound the first range ends just before 12:00, so the ranges are adjacent, not overlapping.

concepts.name: Full-text search
concepts.summary: Search natural-language text with tsvector, tsquery, ranking and a GIN index, without a separate search engine.
concepts.why: Built-in full-text search covers many product search needs with no extra infrastructure.
concepts.body:
`LIKE` matches characters; **full-text search** matches *words*, understanding stemming ("running" matches "run"), ignoring stop words, and ranking results.

- A **tsvector** is a document processed into normalised lexemes with positions: `to_tsvector('english', 'The cats are running')` gives `'cat':2 'run':4`.
- A **tsquery** is a search condition: `to_tsquery('english', 'cat & run')`. For user input use `websearch_to_tsquery`, which understands `"quoted phrases"`, `or`, and `-excluded` like a search box and never raises a syntax error.
- `@@` tests a match; `ts_rank` or `ts_rank_cd` scores it; `ts_headline` builds a snippet with highlighted terms.

For speed, store the tsvector in a **generated column** and index it with GIN, so it isn't recomputed per row at query time. Use `setweight` to rank title matches above body matches.

The text search configuration (`english`, `simple`, `russian`, ...) decides the parser, stemmer and stop words; use the same one for documents and queries. `simple` does no stemming and works for any language, including names and codes.

Limits: no typo tolerance (combine with `pg_trgm` similarity), basic relevance tuning, and no faceting engine. When you need those at scale, a dedicated search engine is the next step — fed from PostgreSQL.
concepts.code:
CREATE TABLE article (
    id    int PRIMARY KEY,
    title text NOT NULL,
    body  text NOT NULL,
    tsv   tsvector GENERATED ALWAYS AS (
            setweight(to_tsvector('english', title), 'A') ||
            setweight(to_tsvector('english', body), 'B')) STORED
);
CREATE INDEX article_tsv_idx ON article USING gin (tsv);
INSERT INTO article (id, title, body) VALUES
 (1, 'Running PostgreSQL in production', 'Backups, monitoring and tuning.'),
 (2, 'A guide to indexes', 'Why the database runs faster with the right index.');

SELECT id, title, ts_rank(tsv, q) AS rank
FROM article, websearch_to_tsquery('english', 'run index') AS q
WHERE tsv @@ q ORDER BY rank DESC;
-- 2 | A guide to indexes | ...   ('runs' and 'index' both match)

SELECT to_tsvector('english', 'The cats are running');   -- 'cat':2 'run':4
takeaways: tsvector = processed document, tsquery = search condition, @@ = match
Store the tsvector in a generated column with a GIN index
websearch_to_tsquery safely parses user-typed searches
pitfalls: Using different text search configurations for the document and the query, so stems don't match.

quiz.q: Why does to_tsvector('english', 'running') match to_tsquery('english', 'runs')?
options: Both are stemmed to the lexeme 'run'
quiz.explain: The English configuration stems both words to 'run', so the lexemes are equal.

concepts.name: Triggers and LISTEN/NOTIFY
concepts.summary: Run PL/pgSQL on row changes with BEFORE and AFTER triggers, and notify listeners with NOTIFY.
concepts.why: Triggers enforce rules and maintain derived data for every writer; NOTIFY pushes changes to apps.
concepts.body:
A **trigger** runs a function automatically when rows are inserted, updated, deleted or truncated. The function is written as `RETURNS trigger` and sees the special variables `NEW` and `OLD` (the row after and before), `TG_OP` (`'INSERT'`, `'UPDATE'`...), and `TG_TABLE_NAME`.

- **BEFORE ROW** triggers can modify `NEW` before it is written (set `updated_at`, normalise values) or skip the row by returning `NULL`.
- **AFTER ROW** triggers see the final row and are used for audit logs, maintaining counters or summary tables, and notifications.
- **Statement-level** triggers (`FOR EACH STATEMENT`) run once per statement; with transition tables (`REFERENCING NEW TABLE AS ...`) they can process all changed rows in one set-based step, which is much faster for bulk changes.
- `WHEN (OLD.status IS DISTINCT FROM NEW.status)` limits when a trigger fires.

Triggers run inside the same transaction, so they're consistent — and their cost is added to every write. Keep them small, avoid long chains of triggers firing triggers, and document them: hidden behaviour surprises developers.

**LISTEN/NOTIFY** is a lightweight pub/sub channel: `NOTIFY channel, 'payload'` (or `pg_notify()`) inside a trigger delivers a message to every session that ran `LISTEN channel`, but only when the transaction commits. Good for cache invalidation; not a durable queue — messages to disconnected listeners are lost.
takeaways: BEFORE ROW triggers can change NEW; AFTER triggers react to final rows
Statement triggers with transition tables are efficient for bulk changes
NOTIFY is delivered on commit and isn't durable
pitfalls: Putting slow work (HTTP calls, heavy queries) in triggers and slowing every write.

quiz.q: A BEFORE INSERT row trigger function returns NULL. What happens?
options: The row is inserted with all NULLs
The insert of that row is silently skipped
quiz.explain: Returning NULL from a BEFORE row trigger skips the operation for that row.

concepts.name: VACUUM and autovacuum
concepts.summary: Why dead tuples accumulate, how autovacuum cleans them, and how to tune it and spot bloat and wraparound risk.
concepts.why: Neglected vacuum is behind most PostgreSQL bloat, slowdowns and the dreaded transaction ID wraparound.
concepts.body:
Because of MVCC, an `UPDATE` writes a new row version and a `DELETE` only marks the old one dead. **VACUUM** reclaims space from dead tuples that no running transaction can still see, so it can be reused; it doesn't normally shrink the file. It also updates the **visibility map** (enabling index-only scans) and **freezes** old rows.

Freezing matters: transaction IDs are 32-bit and wrap around. Rows must be frozen before their xid gets too old, or PostgreSQL will eventually refuse writes to protect data. Autovacuum runs anti-wraparound vacuums automatically; your job is not to block them.

**Autovacuum** launches workers per table when dead tuples exceed `autovacuum_vacuum_threshold + autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor * reltuples` (defaults 50 + 20%). For large tables 20% is far too lazy; lower the scale factor per table: `ALTER TABLE events SET (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.01)`. It also runs `ANALYZE` to refresh statistics.

What stops vacuum from cleaning: long-running transactions, sessions idle in transaction, abandoned replication slots and prepared transactions — they hold back the "oldest xmin". Monitor `pg_stat_user_tables` (`n_dead_tup`, `last_autovacuum`) and `pg_stat_activity`.

`VACUUM FULL` rewrites the table to give space back to the OS but takes an exclusive lock for the whole time; tools like `pg_repack` do it online.
takeaways: UPDATE and DELETE leave dead tuples that VACUUM makes reusable
Lower autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor for large tables
Long transactions and stale replication slots block cleanup
pitfalls: Disabling autovacuum to 'save resources' and later facing bloat or wraparound shutdown.

quiz.q: Autovacuum is running but dead tuples keep growing on all tables. What's a likely cause?
options: A long-running or idle-in-transaction session holding back the xmin horizon
quiz.explain: VACUUM can only remove versions no transaction can see; an old open transaction pins them.

concepts.name: Locks, blocking and job queues
concepts.summary: Find who blocks whom with pg_stat_activity and pg_blocking_pids, and build job queues with SKIP LOCKED.
concepts.why: When the app hangs, the cause is usually a lock chain you can find in a minute with the right query.
concepts.body:
Every statement takes locks. Ordinary reads and writes take weak table locks that don't conflict with each other, plus row locks for modified rows. Schema changes take `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE`, which conflicts with everything — including plain `SELECT`.

Lock waits **queue**: if `ALTER TABLE` waits behind a long transaction, every new query on that table then waits behind the `ALTER TABLE`. That's how a "quick migration" takes down an application. Defence: `SET lock_timeout = '3s'` before DDL, and retry.

To diagnose a hang:

- `pg_stat_activity` shows every session: `state` (`active`, `idle in transaction`), `wait_event_type` (`Lock` means waiting on a lock), `xact_start` and the current `query`.
- `pg_blocking_pids(pid)` returns the sessions blocking a given one.
- `pg_locks` has the raw lock table.
- `pg_cancel_backend(pid)` cancels a query; `pg_terminate_backend(pid)` ends the session.

Row-level locking clauses: `FOR UPDATE` (will modify), `FOR NO KEY UPDATE` (weaker, used by ordinary updates), `FOR SHARE`. Add `NOWAIT` to fail immediately, or **`SKIP LOCKED`** to skip rows other sessions hold. `SKIP LOCKED` turns a table into a reliable concurrent job queue: each worker claims different rows without blocking the others.

Set `log_lock_waits = on` so waits longer than `deadlock_timeout` are logged.
takeaways: Lock waits queue: DDL behind a long transaction blocks everyone after it
pg_stat_activity + pg_blocking_pids find the blocker
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED builds safe concurrent job queues
pitfalls: Terminating the blocked session instead of the one holding the lock.

quiz.q: Several workers run SELECT ... LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED on a job table at once. What happens?
options: They all get the same row and wait
All but one get an error
Each gets a different unlocked row without waiting
quiz.explain: SKIP LOCKED ignores rows locked by others, so each worker claims a different job.

concepts.name: Declarative partitioning in practice
concepts.summary: Partition large tables by range, attach and detach partitions concurrently, and keep pruning working.
concepts.why: Partitioning makes retention instant and keeps huge time-series tables manageable, if you avoid its traps.
concepts.body:
`PARTITION BY RANGE | LIST | HASH` turns a table into a parent with no storage of its own; rows are routed to child partitions. Practical points beyond the basics:

- **Create partitions ahead of time** (a scheduled job or the `pg_partman` extension). Inserts with no matching partition fail, unless you add a `DEFAULT` partition — which then must be scanned when new partitions are attached, so keep it empty.
- **Indexes** created on the parent are created on every partition automatically. A primary key or unique constraint must **include the partition key**, because uniqueness is only enforced within each partition.
- **Retention**: `ALTER TABLE ... DETACH PARTITION ... CONCURRENTLY` then `DROP TABLE` removes a month of data instantly, with no bloat — far better than a mass `DELETE`.
- **Loading**: build and index a table separately, add a matching `CHECK` constraint, then `ATTACH PARTITION`; the check lets PostgreSQL skip validating the rows.
- **Pruning** happens at planning time for constants and at execution time for parameters; it only works when the `WHERE` clause constrains the partition key directly.

Don't over-partition: thousands of partitions slow planning and use more memory. Partitions of a few GB to tens of GB are typical. Partitioning helps maintenance and pruning; it doesn't make single-row lookups by an indexed key faster.
takeaways: Create partitions in advance; keep any DEFAULT partition empty
Unique keys must include the partition key
DETACH ... CONCURRENTLY + DROP is instant, bloat-free retention
pitfalls: Querying by a function of the partition key (date(created_at) = ...), which defeats pruning.

quiz.q: Why must the primary key of a partitioned table include the partition key?
options: PostgreSQL requires every column in the key
Uniqueness is enforced only within each partition's own index
quiz.explain: There is no global index, so only a key containing the partition key is guaranteed unique overall.

concepts.name: Row-level security
concepts.summary: Restrict which rows each role or tenant can see and change with policies enforced by the database.
concepts.why: RLS gives multi-tenant isolation that a forgotten WHERE clause in application code can't break.
concepts.body:
**Row-level security** (RLS) adds per-row filters enforced by PostgreSQL itself. Enable it on a table with `ALTER TABLE t ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY`; from then on, roles subject to it see **no rows** until a policy allows them.

A **policy** has:

- a command (`FOR SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE` or `ALL`),
- target roles (`TO app`),
- `USING (expr)`: which existing rows are visible or can be updated/deleted,
- `WITH CHECK (expr)`: which new or modified rows are allowed to be written.

Policies are combined with OR (permissive, the default) or AND (`AS RESTRICTIVE`).

A common multi-tenant pattern: the application sets a session variable per request, `SET app.tenant_id = '42'` (or `set_config('app.tenant_id', '42', true)` inside the transaction), and the policy compares `tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::int`. With a connection pool, use the transaction-local form so a value can't leak to the next request.

Important exemptions: **superusers** and roles with `BYPASSRLS` ignore RLS, and so does the **table owner** unless you add `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY`. So the application must not connect as the owner. Index the columns used in policies; the policy predicate is added to every query, and functions in it should be simple and leakproof-friendly.
takeaways: ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY + policies filter rows for every query
USING filters visible rows; WITH CHECK validates written rows
Owners and superusers bypass RLS unless FORCE is set
pitfalls: Testing RLS as the table owner or a superuser and concluding it works (or doesn't).

quiz.q: RLS is enabled with a USING policy, but the app still sees every tenant's rows. What's the most likely cause?
options: The app connects as the table owner or a superuser
The policy has no WITH CHECK
quiz.explain: Owners (without FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY) and superusers are exempt from policies.

concepts.name: Extensions and pg_stat_statements
concepts.summary: Install extensions with CREATE EXTENSION and find your most expensive queries with pg_stat_statements.
concepts.why: pg_stat_statements is the first tool to reach for in performance work, and extensions are PostgreSQL's superpower.
concepts.body:
PostgreSQL is built to be extended: new types, functions, operators, index methods and background workers can be packaged as **extensions**. `CREATE EXTENSION name` installs one into the current database (the files must be present on the server); `\dx` lists installed ones. Well-known extensions:

- **pg_stat_statements**: query statistics (bundled with PostgreSQL).
- **PostGIS**: geospatial types and functions.
- **pgvector**: vector similarity search for embeddings.
- **pg_trgm**, **btree_gist**, **pgcrypto**, **postgres_fdw**: bundled contrib modules.
- **pg_cron**, **pg_partman**, **TimescaleDB**, **Citus**: scheduling, partition management, time series, sharding.

Managed services allow a curated list. Updating: `ALTER EXTENSION name UPDATE`.

**pg_stat_statements** aggregates every normalised statement (constants replaced by `$1`): number of calls, total and mean execution time, rows, and buffer usage. It must be in `shared_preload_libraries` (needs a restart), then `CREATE EXTENSION pg_stat_statements`.

The most useful query sorts by `total_exec_time`: the statements that consume the most server time overall, which is often a fast query called millions of times rather than the slowest single one. Reset with `pg_stat_statements_reset()` before and after a change to measure it. Combine with `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` on the top offenders.
concepts.code:
-- postgresql.conf (restart needed):
--   shared_preload_libraries = 'pg_stat_statements'
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_stat_statements;

SELECT left(query, 60)                       AS query,
       calls,
       round(total_exec_time::numeric, 1)    AS total_ms,
       round(mean_exec_time::numeric, 2)     AS mean_ms,
       shared_blks_hit + shared_blks_read    AS buffers
FROM pg_stat_statements
ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC
LIMIT 10;
-- SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = $1 | 1840221 | 95310.4 | 0.05 | ...

SELECT extname, extversion FROM pg_extension;
takeaways: CREATE EXTENSION installs packaged features per database
pg_stat_statements needs shared_preload_libraries and a restart
Sort by total_exec_time to find what really costs the most
pitfalls: Optimising only the slowest single query while a cheap query called millions of times dominates load.

quiz.q: Which ordering of pg_stat_statements best reveals what consumes the most server time overall?
quiz.explain: Total time accounts for both how slow and how frequent a statement is.

concepts.name: Heap storage, TOAST and HOT updates
concepts.summary: How rows live in 8 kB heap pages, how TOAST stores big values, and how HOT updates avoid index writes.
concepts.why: These internals explain table bloat, update performance and why fillfactor and column choices matter.
concepts.body:
Each table is a **heap**: a file of 8 kB pages. A page has a header, an array of **line pointers**, and tuples growing from the end. Each tuple has a ~23-byte header containing `xmin` and `xmax` (the inserting and deleting transaction ids that MVCC uses for visibility). A row's physical address is its **ctid** `(page, item)`; you can select it, and it changes on every update.

Rows must fit in a page, so large values are handled by **TOAST**: values over about 2 kB are compressed (pglz, or lz4 if configured) and, if still large, moved to a separate TOAST table in chunks, leaving a pointer in the row. Selecting only the columns you need avoids de-TOASTing big values.

An `UPDATE` writes a new tuple version. Normally every index must then get a new entry pointing at it — costly with many indexes. A **HOT** (heap-only tuple) update avoids that when two conditions hold: no indexed column changed, and the new version fits on the **same page**. The old tuple then points to the new one, and indexes stay untouched; pruning cleans the chain later without a full VACUUM.

To get more HOT updates on frequently updated tables, lower the **fillfactor** (e.g. 80–90) so pages keep free space, and avoid indexing columns that change often (like `updated_at`). Check the ratio with `n_tup_hot_upd` vs `n_tup_upd` in `pg_stat_user_tables`.
takeaways: Rows live in 8 kB pages; xmin/xmax drive MVCC visibility
TOAST compresses and moves large values out of line
HOT updates skip index writes if no indexed column changes and the page has room
pitfalls: Indexing a frequently updated column like updated_at, which prevents HOT updates.

quiz.q: Which change makes an UPDATE ineligible for a HOT update?
quiz.explain: If any indexed column changes, the indexes need new entries, so the update can't be heap-only.

concepts.name: WAL archiving and point-in-time recovery
concepts.summary: Physical backups with pg_basebackup plus archived WAL let you restore to any moment, not just the last dump.
concepts.why: PITR is how you recover from 'someone ran DELETE without WHERE at 14:03' with minutes of data loss.
concepts.body:
Every change is written to the **write-ahead log** (WAL) before data pages, in 16 MB segment files. Checkpoints periodically flush dirty pages so older WAL can be recycled. That same log enables **point-in-time recovery** (PITR):

1. Take a **base backup**, a physical copy of the data directory made while the server runs: `pg_basebackup -D /backups/base -Ft -z -X stream`. PostgreSQL 17 adds incremental base backups (`--incremental`, combined later with `pg_combinebackup`).
2. **Archive WAL** continuously: set `wal_level = replica`, `archive_mode = on` and an `archive_command` (or `archive_library`) that copies each finished segment to safe storage.
3. To recover, restore the base backup, set `restore_command` to fetch archived segments, set `recovery_target_time = '2026-05-03 14:02:00+00'`, create `recovery.signal`, and start the server. It replays WAL up to the target and stops, then you promote it.

Tools such as **pgBackRest**, **Barman** and **WAL-G** handle the details: parallel and incremental backups, compression, encryption, retention, and verification. Use one rather than hand-written scripts.

Key settings: `archive_timeout` bounds how much WAL (and so data) sits un-archived on a quiet server. Monitor `pg_stat_archiver` for failures — a failing `archive_command` makes WAL pile up until the disk fills.

Physical backups are tied to the major version and the whole cluster; keep logical dumps too for portability.
concepts.code:
# postgresql.conf
#   wal_level = replica
#   archive_mode = on
#   archive_command = 'test ! -f /archive/%f && cp %p /archive/%f'
#   archive_timeout = 60

pg_basebackup -h db1 -U replicator -D /backups/base_2026_05_03 -Ft -z -X stream -P

# --- disaster: bad DELETE at 14:03, restore to 14:02 on a new server ---
tar -xzf /backups/base_2026_05_03/base.tar.gz -C /var/lib/postgresql/18/main
cat >> /var/lib/postgresql/18/main/postgresql.auto.conf <<'EOF'
restore_command = 'cp /archive/%f %p'
recovery_target_time = '2026-05-03 14:02:00+00'
recovery_target_action = 'pause'
EOF
touch /var/lib/postgresql/18/main/recovery.signal
pg_ctl -D /var/lib/postgresql/18/main start
# inspect the data, then: SELECT pg_wal_replay_resume(); to finish and promote
takeaways: Base backup + archived WAL = restore to any point in time
Use pgBackRest, Barman or WAL-G rather than custom scripts
Monitor pg_stat_archiver; a broken archive_command fills the disk
pitfalls: Archiving WAL without ever doing a test recovery to a target time.

quiz.q: What does a PITR restore need besides the base backup?
options: A pg_dump from the same day
All archived WAL segments from the backup's start to the recovery target
quiz.explain: Recovery replays every WAL segment from the base backup's start position up to the target time.

concepts.name: Streaming and logical replication
concepts.summary: Run hot standbys with streaming replication and replication slots, and replicate selected tables logically.
concepts.why: Replicas give high availability and read scaling; logical replication enables near-zero-downtime upgrades.
concepts.body:
**Streaming (physical) replication** ships WAL from the primary to standbys that replay it byte for byte. A standby created with `pg_basebackup -R` (writes `primary_conninfo` and `standby.signal`) follows continuously and, with `hot_standby = on`, serves read-only queries. It replicates the whole cluster and requires the same major version.

- `synchronous_standby_names` makes commits wait for chosen standbys (`synchronous_commit` controls how far: `remote_write`, `on`, `remote_apply`).
- **Replication slots** make the primary keep WAL until a standby has received it. Without a slot a lagging standby can fall too far behind; with an abandoned slot, WAL accumulates until the disk fills. Set `max_slot_wal_keep_size` as a safety cap.
- Long queries on a standby can conflict with replay; `hot_standby_feedback` avoids cancellations at the cost of bloat on the primary.
- Failover (promoting a standby with `pg_promote()`) is usually automated by **Patroni** or a managed service.

**Logical replication** decodes WAL into row changes and sends them per table: `CREATE PUBLICATION` on the source, `CREATE SUBSCRIPTION` on the target. Source and target can be different major versions and have different indexes or extra tables, which enables low-downtime **major upgrades**, consolidating databases and feeding change data capture (Debezium). It doesn't replicate DDL or sequence values, so apply schema changes on both sides and sync sequences at cutover.

Monitor `pg_stat_replication` and `pg_replication_slots` for lag and inactive slots.
concepts.code:
-- on the source (wal_level = logical)
CREATE PUBLICATION shop_pub FOR TABLE orders, customer;

-- on the target, after creating the same tables
CREATE SUBSCRIPTION shop_sub
    CONNECTION 'host=old-db dbname=shop user=replicator password=secret'
    PUBLICATION shop_pub;            -- copies existing rows, then streams changes

-- on the primary: replica lag and slot health
SELECT application_name, state, sync_state,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), replay_lsn)) AS lag
FROM pg_stat_replication;

SELECT slot_name, active,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn)) AS retained
FROM pg_replication_slots;            -- inactive slot + growing retained = danger
takeaways: Streaming replication copies the whole cluster for HA and read replicas
Slots retain WAL for consumers; abandoned slots fill disks
Logical replication works per table across major versions
pitfalls: Leaving an inactive replication slot behind after decommissioning a replica.

quiz.q: Why is logical replication used for major-version upgrades with little downtime?
options: It can replicate between different major versions while the old server stays live
quiz.explain: Logical replication sends row changes, so a new-version server can follow the old one until cutover.

concepts.name: Memory settings and connection pooling
concepts.summary: Size shared_buffers, work_mem and max_connections sensibly, and put PgBouncer in front of many clients.
concepts.why: Mis-sized memory and too many connections are the most common configuration causes of poor performance.
concepts.body:
PostgreSQL uses a **process per connection**. Each backend costs memory and adds contention, so throughput peaks at a modest number of *active* connections (often a few times the CPU core count) and degrades beyond it.

Key memory settings:

- `shared_buffers`: PostgreSQL's page cache shared by all backends. Typical start: ~25% of RAM. The OS page cache holds much of the rest, which is why `effective_cache_size` (a planner hint, not an allocation) is set to ~50–75% of RAM.
- `work_mem`: memory *per sort or hash operation*, per query node, per parallel worker. A complex query can use several multiples of it, times every connection, so the global value stays modest (4–64 MB) and you raise it per session or role for reporting jobs.
- `maintenance_work_mem`: for VACUUM, CREATE INDEX; larger values speed them up.
- `max_connections`: keep it in the hundreds, not thousands.

Other first-pass settings: `random_page_cost = 1.1` on SSDs, `checkpoint_timeout`/`max_wal_size` to spread checkpoints, and PostgreSQL 18's `io_method` for asynchronous I/O.

**Connection pooling**: application pools are per process, and with many app instances or serverless functions the total explodes. **PgBouncer** in **transaction mode** multiplexes thousands of client connections onto a small server pool. Trade-off: session state (session-level `SET`, advisory locks, `LISTEN`) doesn't carry across transactions; recent PgBouncer versions support protocol-level prepared statements.
concepts.code:
# postgresql.conf for a dedicated 32 GB, 8-core SSD server (starting point)
shared_buffers = 8GB
effective_cache_size = 24GB
work_mem = 32MB
maintenance_work_mem = 1GB
max_connections = 200
random_page_cost = 1.1
max_wal_size = 8GB

# pgbouncer.ini
[databases]
shop = host=127.0.0.1 port=5432 dbname=shop
[pgbouncer]
listen_port = 6432
pool_mode = transaction
max_client_conn = 5000
default_pool_size = 40
takeaways: shared_buffers ~25% of RAM; effective_cache_size is only a planner hint
work_mem applies per operation, per connection: keep it modest globally
Use PgBouncer in transaction mode when clients vastly outnumber useful connections
pitfalls: Setting max_connections to 5000 instead of pooling, and degrading throughput under load.

quiz.q: Why is a global work_mem of 1GB dangerous?
options: Each sort or hash in each connection may use up to 1GB, exhausting RAM
quiz.explain: work_mem is a per-operation limit, so concurrent queries can multiply it many times over.
